c.tagline: A living Silk Road museum of madrasas, minarets and turquoise domes.

taxi.fareNote: Street taxis are unmarked and unmetered — agree the fare before getting in, or book a fixed price through Yandex Go.

emergency.note: Fire is 101 and gas emergencies are 104; 112 also works as a general emergency line.

avoid.reason: Nothing beyond bazaar overcharging and taxi haggling — agree prices before setting off.

hood_desc: The walkable heart of the old town, wrapped around the Lyab-i Hauz pool and its shaded chaikhanas, madrasas and the Nadir Divan-Begi ensemble; the natural base for first-timers with everything within a few minutes' stroll.

The monumental core around the Po-i-Kalyan complex — the towering 12th-century Kalyan Minaret, Kalyan Mosque and Mir-i-Arab Madrasa — plus the covered trading domes (taqi) and Ulugh Beg and Abdulaziz Khan madrasas; the densest concentration of Bukhara's UNESCO sights.
The atmospheric old Jewish mahalla of narrow lanes and traditional courtyard houses near Lyab-i Hauz, home to a historic synagogue; a quiet, authentic pocket of everyday Bukhara.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water; the tap supply is not reliable for visitors.

transit.hours: City buses and marshrutka minibuses run roughly 6:00 AM to 9:00 PM; Yandex Go and street taxis cover late-night trips.
transit.note: Bukhara has no metro or tram. The UNESCO old town is small and best explored on foot; buses, marshrutkas and cheap taxis link the historic core with the newer districts and the railway station at nearby Kagan.
transit.pay: Bus and marshrutka fares are paid in cash to the driver (around 1,700 so'm); taxis are cheap but unmetered, so agree the price first or use Yandex Go. There is no rechargeable transit card.

landmarks: Po-i-Kalyan Complex and Kalyan Minaret
The 47-meter 'Tower of Death' minaret, so beautiful Genghis Khan spared it, presides over Bukhara's magnificent ensemble of mosque and turquoise-domed madrasa.
Ark of Bukhara
This massive raised fortress, home to Bukhara's emirs for over a millennium, encloses coronation courts, mosques and museums behind monumental sloping walls.
Lyab-i Hauz
Bukhara's social heart since 1620, a mulberry-shaded pool framed by grand madrasas, teahouses and the whimsical statue of folk hero Hoja Nasruddin.
Samanid Mausoleum
A tenth-century cube of intricately patterned brickwork, among the finest early Islamic buildings anywhere, marking the tomb of the Samanid dynasty's founder.
Mir-i-Arab Madrasa
Facing the Kalyan Mosque across a ceremonial square, this still-functioning sixteenth-century seminary dazzles with twin ribbed domes of brilliant blue.
Chor Minor
A quirky 1807 gatehouse whose four turquoise-capped towers, each uniquely decorated, hide in the old town's lanes like a miniature fairy-tale mosque.
Trading Domes (Toki Zargaron, Toki Sarrofon, Toki Telpak Furushon)
Silk Road commerce survives under these domed sixteenth-century bazaar crossroads, where jewelers, hat sellers and carpet merchants still trade beneath ancient brick vaults.
Bolo Hauz Mosque
The emir's Friday mosque of 1712 mirrors its twenty slender carved-wood columns in a reflecting pool, earning the nickname 'Mosque of Forty Pillars'.
Sitorai Mokhi-Khosa (Summer Palace)
The last emir's 'Palace of Moon-like Stars' blends Russian and Bukharan decadence, with a peacock-stalked garden and dazzling White Hall of mirrored plasterwork.
Chashma-Ayub Mausoleum
Legend says the prophet Job struck a healing spring here; the conical-domed mausoleum above the well now houses a small water museum.

train.note: Afrosiyob high-speed and Sharq/express trains from Bukhara (Kagan) station reach Samarkand in about 1.5 hours and Tashkent in around 4 hours; trains also run west toward Urgench/Khiva.

bus.note: Shared taxis and marshrutka minibuses depart from Bukhara's bus stations for Samarkand, Khiva/Urgench and Tashkent; shared taxis are faster and leave when full.

ferry.note: Bukhara is a desert oasis city in doubly landlocked Uzbekistan, hundreds of kilometres from any navigable water, so no passenger boat services of any kind exist.

full.blurb: A Silk Road town about 45 km away famous for its centuries-old family ceramics workshops and lively bazaar, often combined with the Vabkent minaret.
full.name: Gijduvan

half.blurb: The last emir's summer palace about 4 km north of the city, a lavish fusion of Russian and Bukharan design set in gardens with peacocks.
half.name: Sitorai Mohi-Hosa Palace

half.blurb: A revered Sufi pilgrimage shrine roughly 12 km east honoring the founder of the Naqshbandi order, with courtyards, a mosque and a necropolis.
half.name: Bahauddin Naqshband Memorial Complex

half.blurb: The 'town of the dead' of the Juybari sheikhs, a peaceful 16th-century complex of tombs, mosque and madrasa about 5 km west of Bukhara.
half.name: Chor-Bakr Necropolis
